paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Have you ever longed for a dose of medicine for your mind? Or some ‘gizmo’ to fire an electric current through your prefrontal cortex to kick-start your brain into action, making you just that bit brighter? Most of us wish we could be a bit cleverer, or a little less dense, at the right time; during a job interview, when taking part in a seminar, or while attending an important meeting with a company client. Well, we might not have to wait much longer. For good or bad, a drug to enhance brain function may soon be a reality, and whether or when we should be allowed to use it could be the next big conundrum of medical ethics.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Huge advances in treating mental diseases mean that techniques for improving brain performance could soon be applied, on demand, to healthy brains, in an entirely new branch of elective medicine. This so-called ‘cosmetic neurology’ could be used not merely to improve thought processes, but also to alter other aspects of brain function such as reflexes, attention, and memory, to accelerate all forms of learning and sharpen reactions. In the future, judges could take a cognitive enhancer to ensure that they retain more information, police facing emergencies could speed up their reactions, and the novelist struggling with writer’s block could clear the blockage with a shot of artificial brainpower.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This may sound fanciful, but what plastic surgery can already achieve for the face and body, cosmetic neurology could do for the brain. Techniques for improving brain response are being worked on with the most laudable medical goals - to fight serious neurological conditions such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases - in just the same way that plastic surgery was pioneered to treat the disfigured victims of warfare. But like plastic surgery, if people want cosmetic neurology, then, doctors will provide it, at a price, whatever the ethical issues involved.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The science of mind improvement is developing at an incredible rate. Advances in brain imaging, molecular biology, and genetics mean that scientists are developing their understanding of the way the brain works, and thus increasing the potential to develop drugs to improve its performance. Already, some 40 potential cognitive enhancers are in clinical development in the United States. Dr. Anjan Chatterjee of the University of Pennsylvania, writing in the journal Neurology, recently gave a warning that cosmetic neurology is on the horizon: ‘This is coming, and we need to know it’s coming.’

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A recent study of pilots using flight simulators found that those given a dose of donepezil, a medication used for treating Alzheimer’s disease, performed markedly better in emergency situations. Another recent test, by the US National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, discovered that sending a small electrical impulse through a person’s forehead could improve verbal skills by up to 20 percent. Also, amphetamines used on stroke patients might theoretically be developed for healthy individuals who want to improve their accuracy or speed, for example, a piano lesson.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Of course, no amount of drugs or electric transcranial stimulation will turn someone into a genius, and pills cannot help you recall something you never knew in the first place. Furthermore, the ethical implications of brain-sharpening drugs are enormous and worrying. For example, people might recollect lots of things best left unremembered. There is a good reason why we forget some things. Other difficult questions will also arise: if pilots are safer on certain drugs, should they be required to take them? If soldiers can be treated to improve battlefield alertness and mental acuity, should this be forced on them? If students can improve exam performance with a dose of this or a zap of that, the test surely becomes unfair. And mind medication is sure to have cost implications: will only the rich be able to buy better brains?

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Medicine is there to improve the lives of those who are sick, but should medical knowledge also be used to enhance the lives of people who are perfectly healthy? Millions have seized the chance through cosmetic surgery to become more conventionally beautiful; how many more would leap at the opportunity to become a little bit brainier? Many of us already use a chemical enhancer every day: coffee, after all, has been used as a pick-me-up for at least four centuries. Perhaps cosmetic neurology will be no more than: a small jolt on a dull day to get the synapses firing. Yet the imminent arrival of what is potentially referred to as the ‘clever pill’ must force the medical profession to address, once again, the distinction between patient and consumer, between curing illness and improving the health.
